questions.stem: The ENVIRONMENT (PROTECTION) ACT, 1986 was enacted as a direct response to which event?

options.option_text: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy of December 1984
The Stockholm Conference on environment in 1972
The Rio Earth Summit on environment in 1992

questions.explanation: Bhopal Gas Tragedy — 2-3 December 1984. Methyl isocyanate (MIC) leak from Union Carbide pesticide plant. ~3,800 immediate deaths; tens of thousands chronic + delayed. Worst industrial disaster in history. The EPA, 1986 was the legislative response — UMBRELLA Act giving Centre wide powers to set environmental standards, restrict industrial activities, require environmental clearance. Empowers MoEF&CC. Distractor 3 — Stockholm Conference (1972) led to Wildlife Act, Forest Conservation Act, etc. Distractor 4 — Rio led to Biological Diversity Act + various international conventions.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The FOREST CONSERVATION ACT, 1980 specifically restricts which activity?

options.option_text: Hunting of wildlife inside protected forest sanctuaries
De-reservation of forests for non-forest use without Centre
Eco-tourism inside the protected forest reserves of states
Fishing in rivers and streams within forest boundaries

questions.explanation: Forest Conservation Act, 1980 — bars State governments from de-reserving any forest land or using it for non-forest purposes WITHOUT prior approval of the CENTRAL Government. Aim: stop massive forest loss in the post-1947 decades. Process: states must seek 'Forest Clearance' from MoEF&CC for highways, mining, dams, etc. Compensatory afforestation made compulsory; CAMPA fund for that. 2023 amendment (Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act) controversially loosened scope to exclude security/strategic projects in border areas. Distractor 1 = Wildlife Act. Distractor 3, 4 unrelated.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The CENTRAL POLLUTION CONTROL BOARD (CPCB) was established under the:

options.option_text: Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act of 1981
Forest Conservation Act of 1980 in India

questions.explanation: CPCB — created by the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. Headquartered in New Delhi. Functions later expanded to AIR pollution by the Air Act, 1981. Sets standards for water + air quality, monitors pollution, issues directives. Functions under the umbrella of MoEF&CC. SPCBs (State Pollution Control Boards) operate at state level. Recent CPCB visibility — Delhi-NCR air-pollution monitoring, GRAP (Graded Response Action Plan), AQI publication.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The NATIONAL GREEN TRIBUNAL (NGT) was established in India by the NGT Act in:

options.option_text: 1995, after the Rio Earth Summit obligations

questions.explanation: NGT Act, 2010 — created the National Green Tribunal as a specialised environmental court. India became the THIRD country (after Australia, New Zealand) with such a court. HQ at New Delhi; benches in Bhopal, Kolkata, Pune, Chennai. Disposes environmental cases within 6 months. Has judicial members (HC judges) + expert members (environmental scientists). Notable orders: ban on 10-year-old diesel + 15-year-old petrol vehicles in Delhi-NCR (2015), Yamuna pollution rulings, halting of various projects without clearance. NGT is expert-driven; criticised by some for over-reach.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY ACT, 2002 of India was enacted to give effect to the:

options.option_text: WTO Agreement on Trade-Related IP Rights
UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Rio 1992
UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
Vienna Convention on Ozone Layer Protection

questions.explanation: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 — implements India's commitments under the UN CONVENTION ON BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY (CBD, 1992 Rio Earth Summit). Three objectives of CBD: (1) conservation of biological diversity; (2) sustainable use of components; (3) FAIR + EQUITABLE SHARING of benefits arising from use of genetic resources. Three-tier structure in India: NATIONAL BIODIVERSITY AUTHORITY (NBA, Chennai), STATE BIODIVERSITY BOARDS, BIODIVERSITY MANAGEMENT COMMITTEES (BMCs) at panchayat level. Aims to prevent biopiracy (e.g., neem, turmeric patent disputes). Distractor 1 = TRIPS (separate). Distractor 3 = UNFCCC (climate). Distractor 4 = Vienna + Montreal (ozone).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: PROJECT TIGER, India's flagship conservation programme, was launched in:

options.option_text: 1947, the year of Indian independence from Britain
2005, after the National Tiger Conservation Authority

questions.explanation: Project Tiger — launched 1 April 1973 by Indira Gandhi government to save tigers (Panthera tigris tigris, Bengal tiger). Started with 9 tiger reserves; today >55 tiger reserves. 2005-06 — Wildlife Protection Act amended to create the NATIONAL TIGER CONSERVATION AUTHORITY (NTCA) following Sariska tiger crisis (where tigers had vanished due to poaching). Latest tiger census (2022, released 2023): ~3,167 tigers in India — about 75% of the global tiger population. India's flagship conservation success story.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in India in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted in the wake of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984) to provide a framework for protecting and improving the environment.

questions.stem: The Wildlife (Protection) Act of India was enacted in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted to provide for protection of wild animals and birds and for matters connected therewith.

questions.stem: National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established under:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The National Green Tribunal was established in 2010 under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 for effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection.

questions.stem: The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 restricts:

options.option_text: Dereservation or diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes without Central Government approval

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 requires prior approval of the Central Government before any reserved forest land can be diverted for non-forest purposes (mining, roads, etc.).

questions.stem: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 in India was enacted to implement which international convention?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 gives effect to the provisions of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) regarding conservation, sustainable use, and access and benefit sharing.

questions.stem: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was the first comprehensive water protection legislation in India. It established State and Central Pollution Control Boards.

questions.stem: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) rules in India restrict activities within what distance from the high tide line?

options.option_text: 500 m (or as specified — the historic CRZ I and II limits vary 100–500 m)

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: CRZ regulations restrict construction and industrial activity within 500 m of the High Tide Line (HTL) for ecologically sensitive areas, with variable limits for different zones.

questions.stem: EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) in India is mandatory under which notification?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: EIA is a process mandated under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the EIA Notification, 2006, requiring project proponents to assess environmental impact before clearance.

questions.stem: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 was enacted to prevent, control, and abate air pollution and to establish boards for carrying out these purposes.

questions.stem: Under the precautionary principle in environmental law, the burden of proof:

options.option_text: Lies with the government to prove harm
Lies with those proposing an activity to show it is safe, not with those opposing it

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The precautionary principle (Principle 15, Rio Declaration) shifts the burden of proof: the proponent of a potentially harmful action must demonstrate safety, rather than critics proving harm.

questions.stem: The 'Polluter Pays Principle' means:

options.option_text: Polluters must pay fines to NGOs
Developing nations pay for pollution of developed nations
Taxes on polluting products pay for health care
Those who cause environmental pollution are responsible for meeting costs of preventing/cleaning up the damage

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Polluter Pays Principle, enshrined in Rio Principle 16, holds that the party responsible for pollution must bear the costs of managing, remediating, and preventing that pollution.

questions.stem: CITES regulates:

options.option_text: International trade in wild animals and plants (plants and animals listed in its appendices)

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) is an international agreement between governments to ensure that international trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival.

questions.stem: The Ramsar Convention deals with:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. Sites on the Ramsar list are Wetlands of International Importance.

questions.stem: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) was released in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: India's NAPCC was released in June 2008 and outlines eight national missions including the National Solar Mission and National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency.

questions.stem: E-waste management in India is governed by:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 (and 2022 amendment) regulate the management of electrical and electronic equipment waste in India, imposing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).

questions.stem: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 is also known as:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling communities (including Scheduled Tribes) to forest land and other forest resources.

questions.stem: The Stockholm Convention (2001) deals with:

options.option_text: Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) such as DDT, PCBs, dioxins

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (2001) aims to eliminate or restrict the production and use of POPs — chemicals that persist in the environment and bioaccumulate in food chains.

questions.stem: Which of the following was the first legislation specifically addressing environment protection in independent India?

options.option_text: The Water Act 1974 — first central environmental protection statute

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is considered the first dedicated environmental protection legislation enacted by independent India's Parliament.
